title: My Smart Home Devices Have Been Secretly Eating My Wi-Fi Data, and I’m Not Alone
gist: A Google server misconfiguration made some Gemini-powered Google Home Speakers download a software update over and over. One Reddit user logged 3 TB in about two weeks, and the WIRED author logged 487 GB in 10 days. Google says the problem is fixed. The author also found an Amazon Ring smoke detector using 22 GB a week, and the piece explains how to check per-device usage on Asus, TP-Link, Netgear and ISP apps.

insights.claim: A server misconfiguration caused some Gemini-powered Google Home Speakers to repeatedly download a software update. One user reported 3 terabytes of usage over a couple of weeks, according to Reddit posts reported by 9to5Google.
insights.speaker: Nena Farrell
insights.so_what: This is a quality-control failure in Google's new Gemini smart-home hardware rollout that could cost user trust.
insights.quote: A server misconfiguration caused some Google Home Speakers to repeatedly download a software update.

insights.claim: The WIRED reviewer's own Google Home Speaker used 487 GB in 10 days, almost as much data as the rest of her household used between August and September. Google says only some devices were affected and a fix has rolled out.
insights.speaker: Nena Farrell
insights.so_what: For users with ISP data caps, a bug like this could cause overage charges.
insights.locator: While it isn't happening to everyone

insights.claim: The author unplugged her Google Home Speaker so she would not hit her 2-terabyte-per-billing-period data cap. Users on metered plans could face costs from runaway device downloads.
insights.speaker: Nena Farrell
insights.so_what: Smart-home bugs carry real costs for consumers, and those costs depend on ISP data caps.

themes.theme: Hidden data use by other smart devices

insights.claim: In the author's home, Amazon devices used 22 GB in one week, about as much as a smartphone, even though the only Amazon device set up was a Ring smoke detector. An unidentified device labeled "WATCH" used about 21 GB.
insights.speaker: Nena Farrell
insights.so_what: Smart-home devices may use unexpected background bandwidth, which raises transparency and privacy questions.

insights.claim: Many routers put per-device traffic data behind subscription paywalls. Eero's free app lists connected devices but not how much data each uses. Asus routers offer a free Traffic Analyzer, TP-Link's Deco and Tether apps show traffic usage, and Netgear tracks only overall traffic.
insights.speaker: Nena Farrell
insights.so_what: Subscription paywalls are a growing monetization tactic for router makers and set them apart from competitors like Asus that do not charge.
insights.quote: There are a lot of routers that have subscription fees and paywalls that can hide this information
insights.locator: There are a lot of routers that have subscription fees

insights.claim: ISP apps such as AT&T's can show which high-volume devices use the most data, although they give less detail than router apps. This is how the author spotted the Google Home Speaker and Ring problems.
insights.speaker: Nena Farrell
insights.so_what: ISPs hold device-level usage data, which they could turn into a consumer-facing feature.
